title: What kind of point is it?
intro: Each case describes a point on a curve. Sort it by what it actually is.

buckets.label: Endpoint extreme
buckets.hint: The derivative never pointed at it

cards.text: The cut depth x = S/6 on the open-box volume V(x) = x(S - 2x)²
Lift-to-drag at C_L = √(C_D0/K): climbing below it, falling above
Where a training loss settles with ∇J ≈ 0 and curvature upward
x = 1/e on the curve xˣ, which falls to it and climbs after
f′(c) = 0, f″(c) = 0, and f′ is positive on both sides
y = x³ at the origin: flat for an instant, rising before and after
x = 6 on x³ - 3x² - 9x + 15 over [-2, 6], where f = 69 and f′ = 27
The highest allowed throttle setting, on a problem whose optimum lies outside the permitted range

debrief:
Two of these buckets exist because the obvious test fails. **Inflection** is what you get when f′ = 0 misleads you: the curve pauses and resumes the same direction, and only the sign *change* — or the fallback first-derivative test when f″ is also zero — tells the difference. y = x³ at the origin is the whole lesson in one curve.

**Endpoint** is the one that costs money. On [-2, 6] the cubic's interior peak is 20 and its actual maximum is 69, sitting at x = 6 where the derivative reads 27 and is pointing uphill at a wall. Any search that only collects stationary points never looks there. This is not a textbook curiosity: constrained optimisation lives at its boundaries, which is why the highest permitted throttle, the maximum legal payload, and the tightest allowed tolerance are so often the answer.
